source.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
source.authors: Adly Templeton; Tom Conerly; Jonathan Marcus; Jack Lindsey; Trenton Bricken; Brian K. Chen; Adam Pearce; Craig Citro; E. Ameisen; Andy Jones; Hoagy Cunningham; N. Turner; Callum McDougall; M. MacDiarmid; Alex Tamkin; Esin Durmus; Tristan Hume; Francesco Mosconi; C. D. Freeman; T. Sumers; E. Rees; Joshua Batson; Adam S. Jermyn; Shan Carter; Chris Olah; T. record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates neuron interpretability with automated explanations and held-out activation prediction, a different measure bearing on V7.
record.gate_note: The paper directly compares explanations of Claude 3 Sonnet neurons and SAE features. Other feature examples, steering results, and cited results do not test the claim versions about neuron-explanation scores.
record.test_reason: Section 2.3 directly assesses Claude 3 Sonnet MLP neurons. It uses manual inspection of 50 neurons, and on 100 random neurons it runs simulation-based automated interpretability (explain, then predict held-out activations) plus a specificity rubric. These results bear on how many neurons in another large dense model have one main job (V2) and on simulation scoring of neuron explanations (V7). The rest of the paper concerns SAE features, not neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but narrow. The paper's main conclusion is that SAEs scale to Claude 3 Sonnet and yield abstract, multilingual, multimodal, causally steerable features. On neurons specifically, the authors conclude that random MLP neurons are less interpretable and less specific than random SAE features: neurons typically fire in unrelated contexts, and features mostly do not align with any single neuron. They note they lack a rigorous ground-truth evaluation of interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses automated explanations and held-out activation prediction, but applies them to Claude 3 Sonnet neurons and SAE features, using Claude 3 Opus and reporting a relative comparison rather than a fraction of neurons with good scores.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported comparison is between randomly sampled SAE features and neurons; the text does not report other tested settings for this evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: For 82% of sampled 1M SAE features, the most-correlated neuron in any preceding layer has Pearson r ≤0.3. Best-matching neurons showed almost no semantic resemblance to the features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Claude 3 Sonnet, most middle-layer residual SAE features are not captured by any single preceding neuron.

fits_no_version.finding: Random SAE features scored significantly more specific than random previous-layer neurons on the Claude 3 Opus specificity rubric.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under an LLM-rated specificity rubric, Claude 3 Sonnet neurons are less specific than SAE features.

record.problems: The model size is not reported. Neuron samples are limited (50 for manual inspection and 100 for automated evaluation); the paper gives only a qualitative relative result for held-out prediction and no share of neurons meeting a stated score threshold. The authors note the lack of a gold-standard measure of interpretability.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results left out. Feature steering, feature surveys, and cited findings do not test the listed neuron-audit versions.

untested.parts: Mixture-of-experts models, trillion-parameter scale, separate positive/negative pole analysis, and any numerical share of single-job neurons.
InceptionV1 cat/car neurons and the recursive-generalization reading.
The causes of messy neurons and the rise in interpretability with better tools or architectures. Notably, the neurons were inspected with the same tools as the features.
Attribution is done over SAE features, not neurons. No neuron-only circuit test.
No comparison between explanations from activating examples and prediction on new text, for neurons specifically.
The fraction of neurons with good simulation scores, and the effect of stronger explainers; only the average versus SAE features is reported in text.

missing.what: Distribution of automated-interpretability (simulation) scores for 100 neurons vs 100 features. A histogram is referenced but its values are not in the text, and it is needed to read the share of neurons with good scores.
Specificity score histogram for neurons vs features (figure values not in text).

record.verdict_notes: Despite the 2026 arXiv stamp, this is Templeton et al. 2024 'Scaling Monosemanticity' (Anthropic), not an original source. The reader's V7 limits_scope label is dropped: the missing minority share is an untested part, not a qualification. A relative average cannot show V7's effect, so r1 is cannot_determine. The V2 challenge is qualitative and caveated. It covers whole neurons rather than poles, and the authors frame neurons through superposition. The essay might attribute the messiness to weak tools (V4), which this study does not test.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole shares and the one-job, two-related-jobs, and not-understood proportions.
The claimed shares across models, architectures, and scales.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons and the proposed pose/recursive-generalization explanation.
The proposed causes of messy neurons and the vision-model interpretability estimates.
Whether attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons explain behavior without a trained replacement model.
Whether explanations that fit activating examples fail to predict firing on new examples.
The paper does not report the fraction of neurons achieving a defined good score or give a numerical score distribution.
